lessons.title: Choosing High-Quality Cabbage Seeds
lessons.body:
Choosing good cabbage seeds is the first step to a healthy crop. Always buy seeds from a trusted agro-dealer or seed company. Look for packets with a label showing the variety name, germination percentage, and expiry date. In Africa, common reliable brands include Seed Co, Kenya Seed, and East-West Seed. Avoid seeds sold in open containers or from roadside vendors, as they may be old or mixed with weeds.

Check the germination rate on the label. Good cabbage seeds should have at least 85% germination. If the rate is lower, you will need to plant more seeds to get enough seedlings. Also, check the production date. Cabbage seeds lose viability after 2â3 years if stored in hot, humid conditions. Buy fresh seeds each season if possible.

Seed size and appearance matter. High-quality cabbage seeds are small, round, and uniform in colourâusually dark brown or black. Shriveled, broken, or discoloured seeds are likely dead or weak. You can do a simple float test: put seeds in a glass of water. Viable seeds sink; dead seeds float. Remove floaters.

Store unused seeds in a cool, dry place. A sealed glass jar with a little silica gel packet works well. Keep it away from sunlight and moisture. In humid regions, store seeds in the refrigerator (not freezer) in an airtight container. Proper storage keeps seeds viable for the next planting season.

Finally, match the variety to your local conditions. Ask your extension officer or experienced farmers which varieties perform well in your area. Some are heat-tolerant, others resist certain diseases. Choosing the right seed saves you money and labour later.

lessons.title: Hybrid vs. Open-Pollinated Varieties
lessons.body:
When buying cabbage seeds, you will see two main types: hybrid and open-pollinated (OP). Hybrid seeds are produced by crossing two parent lines. They give uniform, high-yielding plants with strong disease resistance. But they are more expensive, and you cannot save seeds from themâif you do, the next generation will be weak and variable. Open-pollinated varieties are traditional types that pollinate naturally. They are cheaper, and you can save seeds for future seasons, but yields may be lower and plants less uniform.

For commercial farming, hybrids are often better because they give consistent heads that market buyers prefer. For example, hybrid varieties like 'Gloria' or 'Copenhagen Market' produce firm, round heads. They also resist diseases like black rot and fusarium wilt. However, you must buy new seeds every season.

Open-pollinated varieties like 'Cape Spitz' or 'Early Jersey Wakefield' are good for smallholders who want to save money. They are also more adaptable to local conditions over time. But be aware: if you save seeds from OP varieties, they may cross-pollinate with other cabbage family crops (broccoli, kale, etc.) and produce poor-quality offspring.

In Africa, many farmers use both. They plant hybrids for the main market crop and OP varieties for home use or seed saving. Consider your budget, market demand, and whether you want to save seeds. If you sell to supermarkets, hybrids are usually required. If you sell in local markets, OP may be acceptable.

Check with local agro-dealers for varieties suited to your climate. Some hybrids are bred for heat tolerance, others for cold. Choose wisely. Remember: hybrid seeds cost more but can double your yield. OP seeds are cheap but need more careful management.

lessons.title: Seed Treatment and Germination Testing
lessons.body:
Before planting, treat your cabbage seeds to prevent diseases and test germination to know how many will sprout. Seed treatment kills fungi and bacteria on the seed surface. A simple method is hot water treatment: heat water to 50Â°C (122Â°F), soak seeds for 25 minutes, then cool immediately in cold water. This kills many seed-borne diseases. Alternatively, dust seeds with a fungicide like Thiram or Captan following label instructions. In organic farming, soak seeds in a 1% bleach solution for 10 minutes, then rinse well.

Germination testing tells you what percentage of seeds will sprout. Do this before planting a large area. Count 100 seeds (or 10 seeds if you have few). Place them on a moist paper towel or cloth, fold, and keep in a warm place (20â25Â°C). Keep the cloth moist but not dripping. After 7â10 days, count how many seeds have sprouted. If 85 or more sprouted, your seeds are good. If 50â84, plant thicker. If below 50, buy new seeds.

Another method: plant seeds in a small tray of sterile soil. Water gently and keep in a warm, light place. Count seedlings after 10 days. This also tests soil conditions.

If germination is low, you can still use the seeds but sow more densely. For example, if only 60% germinate, sow twice as many seeds as recommended. This ensures enough seedlings.

Always treat seeds before sowing to give them a healthy start. Combine treatment with germination testing for best results. In Africa, where seed quality can vary, these steps save time and money. Do not skip them.

lessons.title: Starting Cabbage Seeds in Nursery Beds
lessons.body:
Starting cabbage seeds in a nursery bed gives you healthy seedlings and better control. Choose a site near water, with fertile, well-drained soil and partial shade. Clear all weeds and stones. Dig the bed 15â20 cm deep and mix in well-rotted manure or compost (2â3 buckets per square metre). Rake the bed smooth.

Make shallow furrows 1â2 cm deep, spaced 10â15 cm apart. Sow seeds thinly along the furrowsâabout 2â3 seeds per centimetre. Cover lightly with soil and water gently with a fine rose can. Mulch with dry grass to keep moisture and suppress weeds. Remove mulch once seedlings emerge.

Water the nursery bed twice dailyâmorning and eveningâusing a watering can with fine holes. Avoid flooding. Seedlings should emerge in 7â14 days. Once they have two true leaves, thin them to 5â8 cm apart to reduce competition. Keep the bed weed-free by hand pulling.

If you use seedling trays, fill with a sterile seed-raising mix. Sow 1â2 seeds per cell, 0.5 cm deep. Water gently and keep in a shaded area for the first few days. Trays are easier to manage and reduce transplant shock.

Fertilise seedlings lightly with a diluted liquid fertiliser (e.g., 1 tablespoon of NPK 20-20-20 in 10 litres of water) every two weeks. Watch for pests like aphids and cutworms. Use neem extract or wood ash as natural repellents. Seedlings are ready to transplant when they have 4â6 true leaves and are 10â15 cm tall, usually 4â6 weeks after sowing. Harden them off by reducing water for a few days before transplanting.

lessons.title: Transplanting Seedlings to the Field
lessons.body:
Transplanting cabbage seedlings at the right time and with care ensures good establishment. Seedlings are ready when they have 4â6 true leaves and are 10â15 cm tallâusually 4â6 weeks after sowing. Water the nursery bed thoroughly a few hours before lifting to reduce root damage. Use a small hand trowel or stick to lift seedlings with a ball of soil around the roots.

Prepare the field in advance. Cabbage needs fertile, well-drained soil with a pH of 6.0â6.8. Plough and harrow to a fine tilth. Add well-rotted manure or compost (2â3 tonnes per hectare) and mix into the soil. If using chemical fertiliser, apply NPK 17-17-17 at 200 kg per hectare during land preparation. Make ridges or flat beds.

Spacing depends on variety. For large-headed varieties, space plants 60 cm between rows and 45 cm within rows. For smaller types, 45 cm x 30 cm. Dig holes slightly larger than the root ball. Place one seedling per hole, ensuring the root ball is level with the soil surface. Firm the soil around the roots and water immediately.

Transplant on a cloudy day or late afternoon to reduce wilting. If the sun is strong, provide temporary shade using leaves or shade net for 2â3 days. Water daily for the first week, then reduce to every 2â3 days. Keep the field weed-free, especially during the first month. Mulch with dry grass to conserve moisture and suppress weeds.

Watch for transplant shockâwilting, yellowing leaves. If this happens, water more and shade. Avoid damaging the roots. With proper care, seedlings will establish within a week and start growing vigorously.

lessons.title: Direct Seeding vs. Transplanting Methods
lessons.body:
Cabbage can be grown by direct seeding or transplanting. Each method has advantages and disadvantages. Direct seeding means sowing seeds straight into the field where plants will grow. Transplanting means starting seeds in a nursery and moving seedlings to the field later.

Direct seeding is faster and less labour-intensive. You sow seeds 1â2 cm deep, 2â3 seeds per hole, and thin to one plant after germination. Spacing should be 45â60 cm between rows and 30â45 cm within rows. Direct seeding works well in warm, moist conditions where seeds germinate quickly. However, you need more seeds, and weed control is harder because cabbage seedlings are small and slow to start. Also, birds and insects may eat seeds or young seedlings.

Transplanting gives you more control. You can start seeds in a protected nursery, water and fertilise them well, and select only strong seedlings for the field. This results in uniform stands and better yields. Transplanting also allows you to prepare the field thoroughly and avoid early weed competition. But it requires more labour: nursery management, lifting, and transplanting. There is also a risk of transplant shock if not done carefully.

In Africa, transplanting is more common for cabbage because it gives higher and more reliable yields. Direct seeding is used in large-scale farms where labour is scarce, or in home gardens where a few plants are enough. If you choose direct seeding, ensure the soil is fine and moist, and keep the area well-weeded. If you transplant, harden seedlings before moving them.

Consider your resources. If you have plenty of labour and want uniform heads, transplant. If you have limited labour and a large area, direct seed. Many farmers combine both: transplant for the main crop and direct seed for a quick second crop.

quiz.q: What is the minimum germination percentage you should look for on a cabbage seed packet?
quiz.explanation: Good cabbage seeds should have at least 85% germination to ensure enough seedlings.

quiz.q: Which of these is a sign of high-quality cabbage seeds?
options: B) Uniform dark brown or black
quiz.explanation: High-quality cabbage seeds are small, round, and uniform in colour, usually dark brown or black.

quiz.q: How should you store unused cabbage seeds?
options: A) In an open paper bag in sunlight
B) In a sealed glass jar in a cool, dry place
C) In a plastic bag in the freezer
quiz.explanation: Seeds should be stored in a cool, dry place in an airtight container to maintain viability.

quiz.q: What is a disadvantage of hybrid cabbage seeds?
options: B) You can save seeds from them
C) They are more expensive and you cannot save seeds
quiz.explanation: Hybrid seeds cost more and their saved seeds produce weak, variable plants.

quiz.q: Which type of cabbage variety allows you to save seeds for future seasons?
quiz.explanation: Open-pollinated varieties can be saved, though they may cross-pollinate with other brassicas.

quiz.q: What is a common hot water treatment temperature for cabbage seeds?
quiz.explanation: Soaking seeds in 50Â°C water for 25 minutes kills many seed-borne diseases.

quiz.q: How long should you soak cabbage seeds in hot water treatment?
quiz.explanation: The recommended time is 25 minutes at 50Â°C, then cool immediately.

quiz.q: What does a germination test tell you?
options: A) The colour of the seeds
B) The percentage of seeds that will sprout
C) The size of the cabbage heads
quiz.explanation: A germination test measures the percentage of viable seeds that sprout.

quiz.q: If a germination test shows 60% sprouting, what should you do?
options: B) Sow twice as many seeds as recommended
quiz.explanation: With 60% germination, you need to sow more seeds to get enough seedlings.

quiz.q: What is the ideal depth for sowing cabbage seeds in a nursery bed?
quiz.explanation: Cabbage seeds should be sown 1â2 cm deep in nursery beds.

quiz.q: How often should you water a cabbage nursery bed?
quiz.explanation: Nursery beds need consistent moisture, so water twice dailyâmorning and evening.

quiz.q: When are cabbage seedlings ready to transplant?
options: A) When they have 2 true leaves
B) When they have 4â6 true leaves and are 10â15 cm tall
quiz.explanation: Seedlings are ready at 4â6 true leaves and 10â15 cm height, usually 4â6 weeks after sowing.

quiz.q: What should you do a few hours before lifting seedlings for transplanting?
options: B) Water the nursery bed thoroughly
quiz.explanation: Watering before lifting reduces root damage and transplant shock.

quiz.q: What is the recommended spacing for large-headed cabbage varieties?
quiz.explanation: Large-headed varieties need 60 cm between rows and 45 cm within rows.

quiz.q: Why should you transplant on a cloudy day or late afternoon?
options: A) To avoid sun and reduce wilting
D) Because it is cooler for the farmer
quiz.explanation: Transplanting in cooler conditions reduces water loss and transplant shock.

quiz.q: What is a sign of transplant shock?
quiz.explanation: Wilting and yellowing indicate the seedling is stressed after transplanting.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of direct seeding cabbage?
quiz.explanation: Direct seeding requires less labour and is faster than transplanting.

quiz.q: What is a disadvantage of direct seeding?
options: B) Harder weed control and more seeds needed
quiz.explanation: Direct seeding uses more seeds and makes weed control difficult because seedlings are small.

quiz.q: Which method is more common for cabbage in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Transplanting is more common because it gives higher and more reliable yields.

quiz.q: What should you do to harden off seedlings before transplanting?
options: B) Reduce water for a few days
quiz.explanation: Reducing water hardens seedlings, making them more resistant to field conditions.

quiz.q: Which of these is a hybrid cabbage variety?
quiz.explanation: Gloria is a common hybrid variety; the others are open-pollinated.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of open-pollinated varieties?
options: B) Cheaper and you can save seeds
quiz.explanation: Open-pollinated seeds are cheaper and can be saved for future seasons.

quiz.q: Why should you not save seeds from hybrid varieties?
options: B) The next generation will be weak and variable
C) They are illegal to save
quiz.explanation: Hybrid seeds are produced by crossing two parents; saved seeds will not have the same qualities.

quiz.q: What is the best way to treat seeds organically?
options: A) Soak in 1% bleach solution for 10 minutes
B) Soak in hot water at 80Â°C
quiz.explanation: A 1% bleach soak for 10 minutes, followed by rinsing, is an organic seed treatment.

quiz.q: How many seeds should you use for a germination test?
quiz.explanation: Using 10 or 100 seeds makes it easy to calculate the germination percentage.

quiz.q: What temperature range is ideal for germinating cabbage seeds?
quiz.explanation: Cabbage seeds germinate best at 20â25Â°C.

quiz.q: What is the first step in preparing a nursery bed?
options: B) Clear weeds and dig the bed
quiz.explanation: You must clear the site and dig the bed before sowing.

quiz.q: How deep should you dig a nursery bed?
quiz.explanation: Digging 15â20 cm deep loosens soil for good root growth.

quiz.q: What is a good natural repellent for pests in the nursery?
quiz.explanation: Neem extract or wood ash can repel aphids and cutworms.

quiz.q: What is the recommended spacing for direct seeding of cabbage?
options: B) 45â60 cm between rows and 30â45 cm within rows
quiz.explanation: This spacing gives plants enough room to grow large heads.
